newsitem.title: EGYPT: Sudan opposition warns foreign firms from Sudan work.
newsitem.headline: Sudan opposition warns foreign firms from Sudan work.

text.p: Sudan's exiled opposition on Sunday warned foreign companies against working with Khartoum and a spokesman said rebels were advancing in the south in their bid to topple the government.

Farouq Abu Eissa, spokesman for the opposition's umbrella group the National Democratic Alliance (NDA), told a news conference that rebel troops were in control of large areas in the south and 50 km (30 miles) from the main city of Juba.
Sudan's government has dismissed rebel claims as untrue and said it was in control of southern positions. On Sunday it said it had recaptured three small southern towns from the rebels.
"In the south the National Democratic forces are on their way to Juba, which we aim to enter," Abu Eissa said.
He was outlining a statement issued by opposition leaders in Eritrea this week on a plan to topple the Islamist government and what they aim to do in the interim after any overthrow.

The latest territory the rebels have seized is at least 1,300 km (800 miles) from Khartoum in Sudan's south, where rebels led by the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) have been fighting the government since 1983.

On Sunday a spokesman in Cairo for the small rebel group Sudan Alliance Forces (SAF) told Reuters the SPLA and SAF killed 100 government troops in an operation near the Ethiopian border on Friday. He gave no figures for opposition losses.
"We have no intention to attack Khartoum itself, but to make available the circumstances for an uprising in cities from north to south," said Abu Eissa.

"One of our resolutions, and this is a decision, is to warn all companies working on contracts with the Sudan government, as well as governments which are helping or assisting the National Islamic Front (NIF) with any money or politically, that we consider all of them hostile to the Sudanese people," he said.
"And as for contracts and agreements, we consider them null and void and will not abide by any of them."
Sudan is one of the world's poorest countries and aims to develop the contribution of gold and oil to the 1997 budget.
This month Sudanese President Lieutenant-General Omar Hassan al-Bashir opened an oilfield developed with Qatari partnership.

Also this month Canada's Arakis Energy Corp AKS.V and its Chinese and Malaysian partners signed final agreements for their $1 billion oil development project in Sudan to develop three blocks. The deal is for 25 years.

"Especially Arakis. If they continue to work there we will come and chase them away with our guns," Gabriel Mathiang, deputy leader of the Sudan People's Liberation Movement, the political wing of the SPLA, told Reuters.
But Abu Eissa said that did not represent the views of the NDA as a whole, which acts as an umbrella organisation for Sudan opposition groups.
"We will not get rid of foreign companies, but we will consider all agreements null and void and we could make new ones with them," Abu Eissa told Reuters. "The NDA would welcome foreign investment."
Sudan also signed a gold deal with a Canadian-registered firm in the northeast, where a French venture now operates.
The opposition has warned before that foreign firms were legitimate military targets.
